lines.speaker: Croesus
lines.text: We can't stand it, Pluto—this dog Menippus living right next door. Either move him somewhere or we'll relocate.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: What harm does he do you? We're all dead here.

lines.speaker: Croesus
lines.text: Whenever we start wailing and moaning about the old days—Midas here about his gold, Sardanapalus about all that luxury, me about my treasures—he laughs at us, calls us slaves and scum. Sometimes he even sings and ruins our wailing. He's a complete pest.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: It's true. I can't stand these base, destructive types. Living badly wasn't enough for them—they have to keep it up after death, still clinging to the world above. So I enjoy vexing them.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: You shouldn't. They're grieving real losses.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You're being ridiculous, Pluto, siding with their groans.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Not at all. I just don't want you fighting.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Well then, you worst of the Lydians, Phrygians, and Assyrians—get this straight: I'm not stopping. Wherever you go, I'll follow, needling you, singing at you, mocking you.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: No. The real outrage was what you did—demanding worship, lording it over free men, never once thinking about death. So now you can wail, stripped of everything.

lines.speaker: Croesus
lines.text: So many great possessions, by the gods.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: That's the spirit. You keep moaning, and I'll sing "Know thyself" over and over. It suits this kind of performance.
